column4: Casement report, chunks 1 to 5: depopulation observed
column5: Casement's report of 11/12/1903 (Africa No. 1, 1904) is a British consul's firsthand account of a 2.5-month journey on the Upper Congo in 1903, comparing places he knew in 1887: Lukolela about 5,000 then, under 600 now (a careful enumeration); Bolobo about 40,000 in early days, now 7,000 to 8,000 (believed); the F* villages 4,000 to 5,000 then, now no more than 500; Montaka 4,000 ten years ago, now 600 to 800; the lake-side towns of Mantumba down 60 to 70 per cent in ten years. These are observed local reductions, not a country-wide count, and he assigns causes jointly: sleeping sickness and smallpox, flight to French territory, hunger, and the methods used to extract rubber and food. This gives the Module 1 toll lesson a primary source for the 'about half' premise at local scale, and for the disease argument. He himself says sleeping sickness takes 'a prominent place' but that natives attribute decline principally to other causes.

Casement says he personally saw two mutilated people at Lake Mantumba: a young man whose hands had been beaten off against a tree, and a boy of 11 or 12 whose right hand was cut off at the wrist; of six mutilated during the rubber regime, five had died by the time of his visit. He also quotes an officer's diary entry (an invalid on his way home, who died soon after) saying that a cartridge expended had to be accounted for by a right hand, and that 6,000 cartridges were used in six months on the Momboyo; Casement 'cannot vouch' for the entry but heard it from an officer of standing. This matches Hochschild's Simon Roi item (finding of 6,000 cartridges) and gives the course a primary basis for 'hand-cutting was a system of proof', with the caution Casement himself uses: first-hand for two cases, second-hand for the rest.

column4: Casement report: how extraction worked, with his own arithmetic
column5: He documents the 'prestations' (weekly and fortnightly food and labour taxes) set by decree (6/10/1891, 5/12/1892, 28/11/1893), the illegal fines imposed on villages, imprisonment of defaulters without trial, the Force Publique estimated at not less than 18,000 men, concession companies with 'droits de police' (Circular of 20/10/1900) and armed forest guards, the A.B.I.R. concession with a yield of 600 to 800 tons in a good year and 58 Europeans, and examples such as one village's weekly levy (value 132 francs, paid 21.30 francs) which he totals over the year: 6,864 francs given and 1,107.60 received (our arithmetic: 132 x 52 = 6,864 and 21.30 x 52 = 1,107.60, both correct). He also reports children sold to pay a fine of 55,000 rods (2,750 francs). Use one case as a worked example of checking an official's figures.

column4: Casement report: his stance and limits
column5: Casement opens by crediting real achievements (steamers, a railway, ending open slave markets) and is cautious about native statements he finds 'of such a nature that I could not believe them to be true' until the people's flight and the facts corroborate; names are masked with letters (A*, B, C) in this printed version, which is the stripping of names that Hochschild says the Foreign Office imposed. Placed beside the course's 'Casement's 1904 report' sentence: the report is dated 11/12/1903, was printed as Africa No. 1 in early 1904, and is a consul's evidence in a diplomatic format, not a court record. It also describes the people as 'savages' and 'cannibals' in the colonial language of its day, which should be flagged to learners.

column4: Casement report: concession system, hostage women and the Wahis circular
column5: At Bongandanga (A.B.I.R. concession) he saw a fortnightly 'market' where 242 men from one village each owed 3 kg of dried rubber (about three quarters of a ton in all; our arithmetic: 242 x 3 = 726 kg), watched by armed sentries, with a 'maison des otages' for defaulters and women seized to force husbands to bring rubber or meat. He puts what a man received for a fortnight's rubber at goods worth under a shilling against rubber worth about 2 pounds (his valuation: 7 kg at 7 francs a kilo), twenty-six times a year. He cites the Governor-General's circular of 29/03/1901 pressing officials to raise rubber yields and says a rifle count shows 550 rifles and many cap-guns for one concession and not less than 10,000 armed men across the concessions, plus a Force Publique of not less than 18,000. This corroborates Hochschild's mechanism (quotas, hostages, concession police) from a primary source and gives the question 'who was responsible' an answer: officials and companies, with the Government 'cognizant and responsible'.

column4: Casement report: African testimony and its limits
column5: Casement records statements from villagers and mutilated children, some taken through interpreters: a 15-year-old boy whose left hand was cut off, which he proved on the spot by confronting the sentry (the one case he could verify and later reported to Coquilhatville), two boys of 6 to 7 with right hands gone, men shot while refusing a rubber levy, and a headman fined 10,000 rods and forcibly moved by the Commissaire-General. He says everything asserted by such people 'strictly true' he would not claim, but that their previous silence said more than their speech. So the report is also a source of African voices, as recorded by a European and an interpreter, which refines Hochschild's remark that few African voices survive in writing. Casement's language ('savages', 'cannibals') is of its time and should be flagged.
